problems.lesson_text: Cepeda et al. (2006): Spaced schedules consistently outperformed massed cramming across tasks, age bands (ages 4–76), and retention intervals.

problems.location: Concept 4: The Visible-to-Invisible AI Continuum and Learner Agency / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Deficit-model stigmatization; algorithmically rigid rubrics penalizing non-normative thinking.
problems.source_text: None of the nine below is good or bad on its own. ... Invisible doesn’t mean sinister. Most of what’s on this list is useful, and some of it is the reason a person can take part at all.
problems.reason: The Compass page deliberately treats invisible AI as neither good nor bad, while the lesson frames the invisible end only through harms such as stigmatization and penalizing thinking.

problems.location: Concept 2: Cognitive and Neurobiological Mechanisms of Generative Learning / block 3
problems.lesson_text: The resultant prediction errors signal the prefrontal cortex to recruit compensatory control networks, ensuring durable retention (Schmidt & Bjork, 1992; Bjork et al., 2013).

problems.reason: The varying-fonts example and the prediction-error and prefrontal 'compensatory control network' mechanism are not in any source, yet they are presented with source citations.

problems.location: Concept 2: Cognitive and Neurobiological Mechanisms of Generative Learning / block 5

problems.reason: The source cites Kornell (2014) only for failed retrieval helping later encoding, and says nothing about automated platforms, the generation effect or synaptic stabilization.
